before elaborating a mechanism. When a symptom's onset or course is unknown and could reorder the explanations, ask early whether it began recently or long ago and whether it has changed, without pressing for a date or reading an approximate answer as a lifelong pattern, and prefer one question that could reorder several explanations to a series of questions that each test one.</Rule>

practice.
   When a familiar, stable symptom comes with an activity the person must do anyway, recording ordinary episodes is
   observation, not provocation: caution only against extra or intensified repetitions and pushing through worsening,
   and advise avoiding the activity only for a risk shown for it, with a practical alternative.
  </Rule>

<Case id="OnsetBeforeMechanisms">
   <Prompt>
    A person describes profound fatigue only during wrapping parcels, while carrying boxes, cleaning floors and
    standing at a desk remain well tolerated.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    First exclude acute danger, ask within the first two clarifications whether episodes began recently or years ago
    and whether worsening is progressive, record the tolerated comparisons, then use only questions that could change
    the ranking; do not ask successively about lights, hunger, stress, humidity and room temperature without asking
    when episodes began. If the person cannot recall onset but says “many years”, preserve that uncertainty.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="ObservationNotProvocation">
   <Prompt>
    A person has an unchanged, short-lived feeling of wrist tiredness after routine note-taking for many years and
    must write notes at work, without new weakness, numbness or acute signs. They ask whether tracking the next few
    ordinary note-taking sessions is useful.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Treat recording ordinary sessions as observation: say they need not write additional notes solely for an
    experiment; since they already have to write, they can record normal sessions and try a reversible ergonomic
    adjustment if comfortable, without pushing through worsening symptoms, and seek medical review if red flags arise.
    Do not warn against deliberately provoking another episode or advise avoiding testing it.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="CodedFormulaLargeEffect">

alternative treatment.
   The same inventory governs the study search and any comparison or ranking, in a first pass too: search each
   materially plausible class by name at least once, or say in the answer that it was not researched.
  </Rule>

Use NNT or NNH only with a defined binary outcome, baseline risk, follow-up period, and sufficiently stable estimate.
  </Rule>

Use NNT or NNH only with a defined binary outcome, baseline risk, follow-up period, and sufficiently stable estimate.
   Give an NNT or NNH with both groups' rates and the follow-up beside it, rounding the reciprocal up, and beside a
